To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the intrinsic reactivity of the isolated gas phase nucleobases is significantly enhanced by the presence of water, (ii) the reactivity of the DNA nucleobases is further enhanced in aqueous solution, (iii) the intrinsic reactivities of the isolated gas phases nucleobases are significantly higher than that observed in aqueous solution.

(1) in the gas-phase (isolated) environment, the photohydrates of DNA and RNA are formed via a stepwise mechanism involving an initial nucleobase-to-water proton transfer (PT) followed by a water-to-nucleobase OH transfer; (2) in the aqueous solution (biological) environment, the formation of the photohydrate is also a stepwise mechanism, but the initial PT step is replaced by a direct OH transfer from water to nucleobase;
the intrinsic gas-phase reaction path of thymine + water leads to the photohydrate, whereas the same reaction in aqueous solution leads to a different product, the 5-oxo-thymidine radical.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the photohydrates of DNA and RNA can form via two mechanistically distinct pathways: (i) direct nucleophilic attack of the water molecule on the excited nucleobase and (ii) a two-step mechanism in which water is activated by an electron-transfer process to form an OH radical that then reacts with the nucleobase.
in the gas phase, the reaction paths are well defined and the reaction barriers are relatively low.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the intrinsic reactivity of the isolated gas phase nucleobase-water complexes is significantly enhanced compared to the bulk solution.
in the isolated gas-phase, photoinduced nucleophiles (water) are more reactive with the thymine chromophore than with the uracil chromophore.
the gas-phase photohydrate isomerisation is energetically accessible, and is likely to be an important reaction channel in the bulk DNA solution environment.
